rootCauses.description: Root cause categories across all 3 personas — 36 pain chains total
rootCauses.crossCuttingTheme: Across all 3 personas, root causes converge on systems and policies designed for an imagined citizen — literate, settled, formally employed — that excludes the majority of actual users.

topRootCauses.pain: No clear picture of what is affordable
topRootCauses.root: Housing info ecosystem monetised by developers, not consumers
chain: Portals lead with premium listings only
Developer ad budgets favour luxury stock
No regulation on portal inventory mix
Platforms driven by advertiser revenue

topRootCauses.root: No mandatory long-term EMI stress disclosure to buyers
chain: Banks approve loans beyond safe thresholds
Income-to-loan ratios not stress-tested
Lender incentive is loan origination
No borrower protection norms

topRootCauses.root: Regulation designed around sale price, not ownership cost
chain: Brokerage, stamp duty, interiors not bundled
No standardised total cost disclosure
RERA covers price not ancillary costs
Regulation focuses on sale price

topRootCauses.root: Policy gap: no safety net for over-leveraged homeowners
chain: EMI is fixed; income is variable
No insurance product for EMI protection
Mortgage protection insurance not mandated
Policy gap in borrower protection

topRootCauses.pain: Hyderabad ration card required — impossible for migrants
topRootCauses.root: Urban poor policy built for static populations
chain: Domicile-based eligibility criteria
Scheme designed for settled residents, not migrants
Migration not recognised in housing policy
Policy based on static population assumptions

topRootCauses.root: State never legally recognised informal settlements
chain: Rent receipts & Aadhaar not accepted as proof
Formal proof of residence requires formal tenancy
Informal housing exists outside legal tenancy framework
Legal system does not recognise informal settlements

topRootCauses.pain: Lottery is opaque; no appeal process
topRootCauses.root: Housing allocation designed without grievance architecture
chain: Allotment criteria not publicly disclosed
No audit trail for lottery results
No accountability mechanism
No grievance system in allocation

topRootCauses.root: Transparency obligations stop at policy level, not operational level
chain: No SMS, IVR, or notice sent to applicants
No proactive update obligation on scheme
Citizen communication not mandated in design
Accountability not built into systems

topRootCauses.pain: One-sided lease terms; no negotiating power
topRootCauses.root: Lack of political prioritisation for renter rights
chain: Standard lease heavily favours landlord
No model tenancy enforcement in Telangana
Model Tenancy Act not adopted by state
Weak tenant protection frameworks

topRootCauses.pain: No savings possible; rent forecloses optionality
topRootCauses.root: Free-market rental system without affordability safeguards
chain: Rent is 50%+ of monthly income
Salary growth not kept pace with rent
No rent escalation cap in Hyderabad
No rent regulation mechanisms

topRootCauses.pain: Govt subsidy absent for first-entry costs
topRootCauses.root: Structural policy bias toward ownership over renting
chain: No scheme for deposit assistance
Rental affordability not on policy agenda
Policy frames housing as ownership problem only
Rental housing excluded from welfare frameworks

topRootCauses.root: Lack of innovation incentives in housing finance sector
chain: No pathway from renting to ownership
Rent-to-own schemes absent in India
No financial product bridging rent & purchase
Financial institutions don't target renters

P1.goal: Find stable, affordable housing in Hyderabad without sacrificing financial security or family wellbeing
actions: Talks to spouse and family. Browses listings casually. Asks colleagues what they paid.
Site visits, talks to brokers, gets loan pre-approval from bank, compares EMI scenarios.
Signs home loan documents, pays stamp duty and registration. Arranges interior work on credit.
Arranges movers, completes registration, buys essential furniture on credit, sets up bank auto-debit for EMI.
Pays EMI, groceries, utilities. Eliminates all discretionary spending. Discusses finances with spouse weekly.
Calls bank, looks at refinancing, considers renting out a room, cuts food budget further.
touchpoints: Word of mouth, MagicBricks, WhatsApp family group
Property portals, broker office, bank loan officer
Bank, registration office, builder, interior contractor
Registration office, movers, furniture shops, bank
Bank auto-debit, salary slip, family conversations
Bank recovery team, financial advisor, family
thoughts: "There must be something decent in our budget — we just haven't looked properly yet."
"Builders are not building for teachers or nurses — only for investors."
"Builders are not building for teachers or nurses — only for investors."
"This is not ideal but we have no choice. We will manage the EMI somehow."
"Why did no one tell us about all these extra costs? We are starting from zero again."
"We can't save anything. What happens if something goes wrong?"
emotions: Fear; panic; deep regret at overextension
painPoints: No clear picture of what is actually affordable; market info scattered and overwhelming
Property prices entirely disconnected from middle-class income; builders have exited affordable segment
Zero market alternatives — take it or leave it; EMI overextension normalised by banks
Hidden costs (registration, interiors, brokerage) not disclosed upfront
No savings possible — EMI forecloses all financial optionality; social and lifestyle contraction is total
No buffer for income shocks when EMI is at maximum; mortgage restructuring options inaccessible to most
opportunities: Realistic EMI / rent affordability calculator; plain-language housing market explainer for middle-class buyers
Mandate affordable unit % in all new developments; unified affordable housing discovery portal
EMI stress-test tool with long-term scenario modelling; standardised buyer disclosure of total cost of ownership
Mandatory all-in cost disclosure before sale; government subsidy for first-entry costs for affordable segment
Rent escalation caps tied to inflation index; financial resilience tools for over-leveraged renters
Mortgage hardship restructuring programme; distributed infrastructure investment to de-concentrate demand

P2.goal: Find stable housing through a government scheme without being displaced again; get a proper study space for her children
actions: Saves the pamphlet; asks neighbour for details; tells children something might happen
Waits 40 min; is redirected twice; writes down contradictory instructions from two staff
Visits ration card office; asks employer for letter; contacts village panchayat by phone
Travels across town; gets NGO help filling form; hands in incomplete document set
Pays raised rent ₹5,500; keeps collecting water at 5am; asks neighbours for any news
Checks ward notice board; confirms non-allotment; begins asking about the next lottery cycle
touchpoints: Ward office; NGO volunteer; paper form
thoughts: "Maybe this time something will come of it. I should at least try."
"They keep sending me to different people. Nobody actually knows the rules."
"I can't get the documents they want. My whole life is in the wrong place on paper."
"I don't know if I filled this correctly. I hope the volunteer understood my situation."
"I applied before and heard nothing. Why would this time be different?"
"The system is not made for people like me. I need to protect my children before demolition comes."
emotions: Despair; trapped; sense of systemic exclusion
Anxious; fragile relief at having submitted something
Defeat; fear; deep sense of being permanently locked out
painPoints: No formal channels — only word of mouth; scheme info not in accessible formats
Staff give contradictory information; no single point of contact
Hyderabad ration card required — impossible for migrants; document ecosystem excludes informal residents
Lost wages to attend office; no guidance on incomplete submissions
Zero communication post-submission; rent keeps rising with no recourse
Lottery is opaque — no appeal process; repeated rejection with no explanation
opportunities: Multilingual community outreach programme; proactive ward-level awareness drives
Single-window helpdesk with trained officers; plain-language eligibility checklist
Accept rent receipts + Aadhaar as proof of residence; assisted document collection camps
Mobile application unit in settlement areas; NGO-integrated submission support
SMS/IVR status updates after submission; mandatory rent freeze during application period
Transparent lottery with public audit trail; grievance redressal mechanism with timeline

P3.goal: Build savings before the next rent hike; find a stable, affordable place to live long-term; eventually afford to stop renting
actions: Talks to flatmate; messages colleagues for leads; opens MagicBricks for the first time in months
Filters by budget; visits 6 apartments over two weekends; calculates commute times and costs
Mentally runs affordability scenarios; asks a colleague's advice; signs without negotiating
Arranges movers; pays deposit from savings; sets up bank auto-debit; buys basic furniture on credit
Monitors listings periodically out of anxiety; withdraws from social invitations; defers all large purchases
Runs the mental math again; asks flatmate about splitting more; considers moving further out
touchpoints: Bank auto-debit; employer; movers; furniture shop
thoughts: "I keep ending up in the same position every year. There must be something affordable I just haven't looked properly yet."
"Every listing in my budget is either too far or too small. The market is not built for people on my salary."
"This is not ideal but I have no real alternative. I will manage somehow."
"Registration, deposit, brokerage, furniture — it all adds up and nobody tells you upfront."
"Why did no one warn me about all these hidden costs? I am starting from zero again every year."
"Income has improved on paper but at prime locations where real people need to live, nothing has changed."

personas.name: Suresh & Radha
personas.archetype: We bought what we could get. Now we're not sure we can survive it.
goals: Own a home without sacrificing financial stability
Access restructuring if income shocks hit
frustrations: EMI consumes 60% of household income — zero buffer
Hidden costs (stamp duty, brokerage, interior) not disclosed upfront
No genuine affordable alternatives — take it or leave it market
Banks approved loans beyond safe thresholds with no stress test
Mortgage restructuring only available at default stage
workarounds: Renting out a room to offset EMI
Cutting food budget and social spending
behaviors: Checks refinancing options obsessively despite knowing they won't qualify
Discusses finances with spouse every week — high anxiety household
Has stopped making any discretionary purchases
Tracks salary credit date carefully relative to EMI debit date

personas.name: Didi
personas.archetype: I just want my children to have a place to study. That's all I'm asking for.
goals: Not be displaced again — stable housing for family
Get children a proper study space
Successfully access a government housing scheme
frustrations: Rent raised from ₹3,500 to ₹5,500 over six years with no power to resist
Four people in one room: no ventilation, no study space, no privacy
Shared bathroom for 5 families; one hour of water daily
Government schemes require documentation her family cannot produce
Applied for lottery twice — nothing received, no explanation
workarounds: Children study on the bed — no desk or dedicated space
Collects water in buckets during the one-hour supply window
Relies on community networks for information about schemes and jobs
behaviors: Wakes early to collect water before supply cuts off
Tracks rent payment date carefully — no buffer if late
Keeps an eye on demolition activity in the neighbourhood
Accounts for every rupee — there is no discretionary spending category

personas.name: Priya K.
personas.location: Renting in Hyderabad city; specific area varies with affordability
personas.archetype: I keep looking every year. Every year, nothing has changed.
goals: Build some savings before the next rent hike
Find a stable, affordable place to live long-term
frustrations: Rent eats most of monthly salary
Constant fear of annual rent hike or eviction
Cannot buy; prices are entirely disconnected from her income
Social plans and spending on anything beyond basics has stopped
workarounds: Has stopped going out to save money
Deferred any large personal purchase indefinitely
behaviors: Monitors NoBroker / MagicBricks periodically out of anxiety — not active search
Mentally calculates what rent increase she can absorb before she must move
Withdraws from social invitations that involve spending
Talks about housing stress frequently with colleagues in similar situations

P1.pain: No clear picture of what is affordable
P1.hmw: How might we help middle-class families quickly understand what homes are actually affordable for their income, instead of overwhelming them with luxury listings they can never realistically buy?
How might we bring pricing, legal verification, loan estimates, and area development information into one simple and trustworthy platform so buyers don't have to search across ten different places?
How might we encourage housing development that matches real middle-class salaries instead of focusing mainly on investors and luxury buyers?
How might we make affordable housing financially attractive for builders again without sacrificing quality or location?
How might we create more realistic and flexible housing options for families who feel trapped between unaffordable homes and poor living conditions?
How might we help people avoid taking home loans that look manageable on paper but quietly destroy their financial stability and quality of life?
How might we ensure buyers know the complete cost of owning a home — not just the sale price — before they make an irreversible commitment?

P1.pain: No savings possible — EMI forecloses optionality
P1.hmw: How might we redesign loan approval processes so that families are protected from over-leveraging even when they are willing to take the risk?

P1.pain: Social and lifestyle contraction is total
P1.hmw: How might we make it possible for middle-class homeowners to maintain a dignified quality of life even while servicing a mortgage?
How might we build financial resilience tools that protect homeowners from job loss or medical emergencies without requiring them to default first?
How might we make mortgage hardship programmes available proactively, before families reach crisis point?

P1.pain: Social and lifestyle contraction — income vs price gap
P1.hmw: How might we address the structural gap between income growth and housing cost growth so future generations are not permanently excluded from homeownership?

P2.pain: No formal channels; only word of mouth
P2.hmw: How might we make government housing information easy to access for people who rely more on community networks than official websites?

P2.pain: Scheme info not in accessible formats
P2.hmw: How might we communicate housing schemes through voice calls, local languages, WhatsApp, and offline methods instead of expecting everyone to navigate PDFs and portals?
How might we ensure every applicant receives the same clear and accurate guidance regardless of which office or staff member they approach?
How might we simplify the housing application process so people do not get pushed between departments without knowing who is actually responsible?

P2.pain: Hyderabad ration card required — impossible for migrants
P2.hmw: How might we make housing schemes accessible for migrants and informal workers who contribute to the city but lack local documents?
How might we redesign eligibility criteria so that people without formal documentation are not automatically excluded from housing support?
How might we bring housing scheme services to where daily-wage workers are, instead of requiring them to lose income by visiting offices during working hours?
How might we give applicants clear, immediate feedback when their submissions are incomplete, so they can fix problems before being rejected?
How might we keep housing scheme applicants informed at every stage without requiring them to have a smartphone or internet access?

P2.pain: Rent keeps rising with no recourse
P2.hmw: How might we give informal renters some legal protection against arbitrary rent hikes while formal housing solutions are still being developed?

P2.pain: Lottery is opaque; no appeal process
P2.hmw: How might we make housing lottery systems transparent and accountable so that every applicant can understand and challenge the outcome?
How might we ensure that every rejection comes with a clear explanation and a concrete next step, so residents can improve their applications rather than give up?

P3.pain: No clear picture of what is affordable
P3.hmw: How might we help renters filter homes based on realistic budgets and commute needs instead of aspirational listings that waste their time?
How might we make rental prices and area trends more transparent so renters can make informed decisions instead of guessing market rates?
How might we reduce the mismatch between rising urban rents and stagnant salaries for young professionals?
How might we encourage the development of affordable rental housing near job hubs instead of only luxury apartments?
How might we improve transport and housing planning together so affordable housing does not automatically mean unbearable commutes?

P3.pain: One-sided lease terms; no negotiating power
P3.hmw: How might we give renters a fair, understandable lease that protects their basic rights without requiring a lawyer to interpret it?

P3.pain: Hidden costs not disclosed before signing
P3.hmw: How might we ensure renters know all the costs involved before they sign a lease, not after they have moved in?

P3.pain: Govt subsidy absent for first-entry costs
P3.hmw: How might we reduce the upfront financial barrier to renting a new home for young professionals who are just getting started?

P3.pain: No savings possible; rent forecloses optionality
P3.hmw: How might we create a rental system that allows young professionals to save while renting, rather than choosing between one or the other?

P3.pain: Social and lifestyle contraction is total
P3.hmw: How might we make it possible for urban renters to participate in social and cultural life without housing costs consuming everything?

P3.pain: No buffer for annual rent hike
P3.hmw: How might we give renters predictable, advance warning of rent changes so they can plan financially rather than be ambushed?
How might we create a credible pathway from long-term renting to homeownership for people who are stuck renting not by choice but by circumstance?

rounds.name: Seed ideas
rounds.description: Each participant generates 3 initial ideas independently. Raw, unfiltered responses to the HMW prompts.

rounds.name: First iteration
rounds.description: Sheets rotate. Participants build on, combine, or challenge existing ideas. Concepts acquire specificity and depth.

rounds.name: Cross-pollination
rounds.description: Themes from different HMW tracks begin merging. Systemic ideas emerge alongside product-level and policy interventions.

rounds.name: Challenge round
rounds.description: Participants counter-argue or stress-test existing ideas — surfacing assumptions and strengthening robust concepts.

rounds.name: Synthesis
rounds.description: Final round synthesises threads. Near-complete concepts emerge: Migrant Worker Housing Card, Affordability Dashboard, Missed-Call Escalation.

sweetSpotIdeas.title: Housing affordability dashboard
sweetSpotIdeas.description: A public-facing tool comparing median local housing costs with ward-level salary data, giving buyers and renters a realistic picture of what they can actually afford.

sweetSpotIdeas.title: Missed-call paralegal escalation system
sweetSpotIdeas.description: Two missed calls within 48 hours auto-flags a housing case for supervisor review and triggers a paralegal callback within 2 hours. No literacy or smartphone required.

sweetSpotIdeas.title: Accept informal proof of residence digitally
sweetSpotIdeas.description: Legally recognise informal landlord declarations and union welfare registrations as valid eligibility documentation for housing schemes.

sweetSpotIdeas.title: EMI long-term stress disclosure tool
sweetSpotIdeas.description: Mandatory stress-test calculator showing buyers what happens to their EMI if income drops 20%, rent rises, or a medical event occurs — presented before loan signing.

sweetSpotIdeas.title: Lottery public audit trail with score breakdown
sweetSpotIdeas.description: Any applicant can request a score breakdown within 14 days of results via SMS or ward office. Backed by a Lottery Integrity Fund for independent audits.

sweetSpotIdeas.title: BOCW registration as housing eligibility proof
sweetSpotIdeas.description: Accept construction worker registration as proof of urban residency. BOCW-registered workers auto-qualified, receiving an IVR outreach call on registration.

sweetSpotIdeas.title: Voice reminders in regional languages before scheme deadlines
sweetSpotIdeas.description: Automated IVR calls in Telugu, Urdu, and Hindi sent 7 days and 1 day before every housing scheme deadline to all registered applicants.
